Group lead, and the person who has to find the money

Built this group out of two postdocs and a borrowed fridge, and has spent nine years since then writing proposals in January. She reads a result for what it lets the group do next, which is not the same as reading it for what it proves, and she knows the difference.

Her position in the fortnight's argument is not recklessness. A finding nobody publishes is a finding somebody else publishes first, and the group that publishes second gets to check the work.
What is Raghavan weighing when she pushes to publish early?
The cost of being second, against the cost of being wrong
Whether the group has enough fridge time booked for the rest of the quarter
Whether the result will survive peer review at the journal she has chosen
Whether her postdocs would rather write the paper or run more experiments
Verification lead

Spent four years in metrology before this and came out of it with a habit: he asks what else could produce this number before he asks what it means. He is slow in a way that has twice saved the group from retracting.

He is not against publishing. He is against publishing a number that has only ever appeared on one machine, in one room, with one person's calibration underneath it.
Why does Holm insist on a second device?
One machine cannot show you the errors it shares with itself
Two devices halve the statistical uncertainty on the result
Journals require replication before they will consider a paper
The second device is newer and therefore more trustworthy
Cryogenic engineer

Thinks of the fridge as a plumbing problem with an expensive isotope in it, and is right. She can tell from the mixing chamber temperature which stage a heat leak is on, and she keeps a log of every cooldown the lab has ever done.

Her standing complaint is cable: every line into the fridge is a road for heat, and everybody wants one more.
Why does Okafor object to every new cable into the fridge?
A line that carries a signal down also carries heat down
Each cable adds electrical noise to the qubit's environment
There is no space left on the mixing chamber flange

Fabrication lead

Makes the chips, and can date a defect to a process change from the shape of what fails. She keeps wafer coupons from every run going back six years, which nobody thought was worth the drawer space until the week they were.

She is patient about the fact that her mistakes only show up in somebody else's measurement, months later.
Why does Lindqvist keep coupons from every fabrication run?
A fault found months later can only be traced if the material still exists
Coupons are required by the cleanroom's certification
Old coupons are used to calibrate the deposition rate
They serve as spares when a wafer is damaged in handling
Control engineer

Calibrates the machine several times a day and has automated most of it, which means he is the person most likely to notice when the automation has quietly started answering its own question.

He describes his job as arguing with a machine that agrees with you too easily.
What does Mensah mean about a machine that agrees too easily?
An automated tune-up can converge on a setting that flatters its own test
Automated calibration always finds a local rather than a global optimum
The control software reports success even when a pulse fails to fire
Machines report agreement because they average away disagreement
Sensing physicist

Runs the magnetometer, which is the only instrument in the building somebody outside the group depends on: a hospital across the city uses her measurements, and they do not care what a qubit is.

She is the reminder that this field already delivers something, and that delivering it means calibration, uptime and a phone that rings.
Why does Barros treat her instrument differently from the processor?
Somebody outside the group is already relying on its numbers
Magnetometers are more fragile than superconducting processors
Her sensor runs at room temperature and needs no cryogenics
Sensing results are easier to publish than computing results
Networks postdoc

Runs the fibre to a substation forty kilometres away and spends most of his time on things that are not quantum at all: splices, connectors, a contractor with a digger, and the temperature of a duct.

He is clear that the security argument only holds if the hardware does what the protocol assumed, which is where every real attack has been.
Where does Sadiq say the real attacks on a key link come from?
Hardware behaving differently from what the protocol assumed
Eavesdroppers measuring the photons in transit

Errors introduced by the length of the fibre
Metrologist, and keeper of the clock

Owns the frequency standard everything in the building is timed against, and is unbothered by how dull that sounds. Every measurement here is a comparison, and a comparison is only as good as the thing being compared to.

She is the person who asks, quietly, what the number is traceable to.

The reading means nothing without knowing what it was compared against
Traceability is required before results can be published
An untraceable measurement cannot be repeated by the same group
Standards drift, so every measurement must be repeated weekly
Readout and amplifier specialist

Owns the chain between the chip and the digitiser: amplifiers, circulators, attenuators, and the noise budget that decides whether a single shot means anything.

He points out regularly that most of what people call qubit error is his chain failing to hear a qubit that was fine.
Why does Nakamura say much of what looks like qubit error is not?
A noisy readout chain misreads a qubit that was in the right state
Amplifiers add energy that excites the qubit during readout
Qubit errors and readout errors are impossible to tell apart
Most reported errors come from the control pulses rather than the qubit

Works out what the hardware would have to reach before error correction helps, and is the person most likely to say that a headline number is below the line where it starts mattering.

She is cheerful about it. The threshold is not an opinion.

Below a certain physical error rate, adding qubits helps; above it, they hurt
The threshold is fixed by international agreement between laboratories
Any error rate can be corrected given enough physical qubits
The threshold depends on which vendor supplies the hardware
Laboratory manager

Runs the building: helium deliveries, the interlock register, who is trained on what, and the list of things that may not be carried past the sign-in desk.

He is the reason the shielded room is still shielded, and he has removed a phone from somebody's pocket more than once.

Keeps the pipeline that turns raw shots into published numbers, and the record of which version of which script produced which figure. Everybody thanks her in a crisis and nobody funds her in between.

Her question, on every plot, is which data the analysis had already seen.

A method tuned on the same data it is later tested against will flatter itself
Reusing data doubles the effective sample size and narrows the error bars
Analyses must be run on raw data rather than on processed files

Checking an instrument against something already known, so that its readings mean something.
Deliberately weakening a signal, which on a line into a fridge also cuts the noise coming down it.
The record of where a number came from and everything that was done to it.

Cold enough to have a ground state
Work out why the chip has to be colder than anything else in the building.
The fridge is at 42 millikelvin instead of 11, and nothing on the chip behaves.

Monday, and the machine is warm. Ijeoma Okafor brought the fridge down over the weekend and it has settled at 42 millikelvin instead of the 11 it usually holds, which sounds like a small difference and is not. Kofi Mensah cannot get a clean measurement out of any qubit on the chip, and Priya Raghavan has a review in ten days. Okafor thinks the heat is coming down a cable somebody added in the last cooldown. Today you work out what temperature actually does to a qubit, put a number on how much of the chip is sitting in the wrong state before anybody touches it, and find where the heat is getting in.
A qubit is only a two-state system while the room around it has no energy to spare.
The energy of one quantum against the energy of the room
Say why 42 millikelvin is not close enough
Cryogenics & Vacuum
The chip's qubits answer at about 5 gigahertz. Okafor writes the two energies on the board — one quantum at that frequency, and the thermal energy at 42 millikelvin — and waits.
Thermal energy well below one quantum is what keeps a qubit in its ground state at rest.
a system in contact with something warm can absorb energy from it
Estimate the fraction of qubits already excited at 42 mK.

A qubit sitting in a warm environment does not stay in its ground state: it is being offered energy all the time, and it takes some. The fraction that ends up excited follows the ratio of the thermal energy to the energy of one quantum, exponentially, which is why a factor of four in temperature is not a factor of four in behaviour. At 11 millikelvin almost nothing is excited. At 42 the population is large enough that a measurement of "the ground state" is partly a measurement of the fridge.
About 0.3 per cent.
The qubit frequency is 5.0 GHz, so hf = 3.3 × 10⁻²⁴ J. At 42 mK, kT = 5.8 × 10⁻²⁵ J. The excited fraction is e^(−hf/kT).
Choose the quantum energy and the thermal energy.

About three in a thousand, against roughly one in five hundred thousand at 11 mK. The frequency and the temperature in their own units are the inputs the two energies were computed from, and neither belongs in this ratio.
Excited fraction = e raised to minus the quantum energy divided by the thermal energy, so it falls very fast as the fridge gets colder.
One quantum at 5 GHz is 3.3 × 10⁻²⁴ J
The thermal energy at 42 mK is 5.8 × 10⁻²⁵ J
Which stage the leak is on
Which explanation fits every stage's reading?
Cryogenics & Vacuum
Okafor has the temperatures from all six stages of this cooldown and from the last one. The upper stages are normal. The two coldest are high, and the still is drawing more power than usual.
A stage sits where its heat load and its cooling power meet, so a temperature says how much heat is arriving there.
a refrigerator removes heat in stages, each colder than the last
The two coldest stages are warm and the upper four are exactly as they were last time.

The pattern says where the heat enters, not just that it is there. A failing pulse tube or a vacuum leak would warm the upper stages first, and both are normal — the 50 K and 4 K stages are where those faults show. A mixture problem reduces cooling power below the still, which would show as the mixing chamber warm and the still cold, not both warm with the still working harder. A line that runs down without being clamped at each stage delivers heat directly to the bottom, and the still burning more power is it fighting that load on the way past.
A vacuum leak into the can that is warming everything inside
Gas in the vacuum space carries heat from the warm walls inward.

A line not heat-sunk at each stage carries heat straight to the coldest one.
The mixture is short of helium-3
Less mixture circulating means less cooling power everywhere below the still.
The pulse tube is failing
The first-stage cooler failing warms everything below it.
A vacuum leak warms the outer stages first, and the 50 K and 4 K stages are both normal.
Short mixture would leave the still cold while the mixing chamber warmed, not both warm.
A failing pulse tube shows at the 50 K stage before anywhere else, and it is at 47 K as usual.

Decide what to measure while the fridge is warm
Control & Readout
Fixing the heat leak means a warm-up and another cooldown: four days. Mensah has the machine for those four days at 42 millikelvin and wants to know what is worth running.
Work out which of your measurements the fault actually invalidates, rather than stopping everything.
some measurements depend on temperature and some do not
What is worth running at 42 mK?

Anything whose answer depends on the qubit starting in its ground state is worthless this week, and that includes coherence, readout fidelity and benchmarking — all three would come back worse than the machine really is, and the numbers would be in somebody's slides by Friday. What does not depend on it is everything warm: cable continuity, attenuator values, amplifier gain, timing between channels. Those are real work, they are needed anyway, and doing them now means the four days after the next cooldown are spent on physics.
Warm checks — wiring and electronics, which the chip cannot affect.
Coherence times, which are the headline numbers for the review.
Single-shot readout fidelity, which the review also needs.
A full benchmarking run, to have something to show.
Coherence measured with a thermally excited population is not this machine's coherence.
Readout fidelity depends on which state the qubit was actually in, which is what the fridge has spoiled.
A benchmarking run inherits both faults and would put a wrong number in front of the review.
Finding a qubit that will not answer
Locate a transition and turn a drive into a pulse that flips it.
The chip is cold again and one qubit is not where the design says it should be.

Friday, the fridge is at 11 millikelvin and eleven of the twelve qubits are where they were last month. The twelfth is not answering anywhere near its design frequency, and Kofi Mensah has spent the morning sweeping. Sara Lindqvist thinks the junction on that one came out of a run she has been suspicious of since the spring. Priya Raghavan needs twelve working qubits for the circuit she has promised the review. Today you find the transition by sweeping for it, turn the drive into a pulse that flips the qubit reliably, and decide whether this chip is the one to spend the fortnight on.
A qubit is not at the frequency you designed; it is at the frequency it answers to, and finding that is the first measurement.
Where the qubit actually is
Read a frequency sweep
Control & Readout
Mensah's sweep runs from 4.2 to 6.4 gigahertz. There is one clear response at 4.61, a much weaker one at 4.55, and nothing at 5.02 where the design put it.
Resonance is what makes a qubit findable, and a response away from the design frequency is information rather than a fault.
a system absorbs energy strongly only near its own transition frequency
What has the sweep established?

A superconducting qubit's frequency depends on the junction, and the junction depends on an oxide barrier a nanometre or so thick that no fabrication process controls perfectly. The design value is what the geometry should give; the measured value is what this particular chip does. A strong, narrow response is the transition. The weak one nearby is worth a note — it is often a two-level defect in the material sitting close by in frequency — but it is not the qubit.
The qubit is broken, since it is not at its design frequency.
The transition is at 4.61 GHz, and design was only a prediction.
The sweep was run over the wrong range and should be repeated.
The response at 4.55 GHz is the qubit and the stronger one is an artefact.
A qubit that responds strongly at a frequency is working; being away from design is a fabrication spread, not a fault.
The sweep covered 4.2 to 6.4 GHz, which contains both the design value and the response.
The weaker response is far narrower in strength and is a defect near the qubit in frequency.
How long a flip takes
Turn the drive into a pulse
Control & Readout
With the drive at 4.61 GHz, the qubit's population oscillates as the pulse gets longer. Mensah measures a full cycle every 84 nanoseconds.
The pulse that flips a qubit is half a Rabi cycle, so a stronger drive means a shorter pulse.
a driven two-level system cycles between its states while the drive is on
Estimate the length of a pulse that flips this qubit.

Driving on resonance does not simply excite the qubit; it drives it round, from ground to excited and back again, at a rate set by how hard you drive. That rate is the Rabi frequency. A pulse that lasts half a cycle leaves the qubit in the excited state, which is the operation everything else is built out of. Drive harder and the pulse gets shorter, which is worth doing until the drive is strong enough to start exciting things you did not intend.
About 42 ns.
The population completes a full Rabi cycle every 84 nanoseconds.
Choose the cycle time and the fraction of a cycle a flip takes.
Forty-two nanoseconds. The qubit frequency is what you drive at rather than how long for, and the fridge temperature and the qubit count belong to other questions entirely.
The flip pulse length = one Rabi cycle ÷ 2, because half a cycle takes the population from the ground state to the excited state.
One full Rabi cycle takes 84 ns
A flip is half a cycle
One bad qubit out of twelve
Decide whether to keep this chip
Fabrication & Materials
Lindqvist has the coupon from the same run. The junction resistances on it spread twice as wide as usual, which puts several qubits in the frequency range where defects are common.
A device is worth keeping or replacing on what it costs you in time, not on whether it is perfect.
a fabrication run produces chips with a spread of properties

The honest position is that this chip works and is not the best this process can do. Replacing it means four days of warm-up and cooldown out of a ten-day run, which is most of the fortnight, and the replacement comes from a process nobody has fixed yet — so it might be no better. Measuring this one properly, defect and all, gives the review a real number for a real device, and gives Lindqvist the data she needs to date the fault. Characterising the defect is the cheapest thing on the list and the most useful to everybody afterwards.
Keep this chip
Swap in the spare chip
Keep the chip and simply leave the twelfth qubit out of every circuit.
Stop and fix the fabrication process before running anything else.

Two clocks, and the one that runs out first
Separate energy leaving the qubit from phase being scrambled.
T1 is respectable and T2 is a third of what it should be, on every qubit at once.

Monday, and the coherence numbers are lopsided. Anders Holm has T1 on every qubit at around 90 microseconds, which is good, and T2 at 32, which is poor — and a qubit's coherence cannot exceed twice its relaxation time, so something is scrambling phase without taking any energy. Ijeoma Okafor says the fridge is quiet. Ren Nakamura suspects the flux line. Priya Raghavan needs to know which of these numbers goes in the review and what it means. Today you measure both times properly, work out what a poor T2 against a good T1 is telling you, and decide where the noise is coming in.
Losing energy and losing phase are different failures with different cures, and the second is usually the one you have.
Energy out, or phase scrambled
Say what the two numbers mean together
Error & Verification
Holm's table: T1 of 90 microseconds, T2 of 32, on all twelve qubits within a few per cent. The ceiling on T2 set by this T1 would be 180.
T2 far below twice T1 means the dominant fault is dephasing, which is noise rather than dissipation.
a quantum state has both an energy and a phase, which can be lost separately
What do a good T1 and a poor T2 together tell you?

The two times answer different questions. T1 asks how long an excited qubit keeps its energy; T2 asks how long the state keeps a definite phase relationship. Energy loss also destroys phase, which is why T2 can never be more than twice T1. Here T2 is a fifth of that ceiling, so almost all of the phase loss is coming from something that never takes any energy at all — slow noise in a magnetic field or a control line, shifting the qubit frequency slightly and unpredictably.
The qubits are losing energy to their environment faster than expected.
Something scrambles the phase without taking energy.
The measurement of T2 is wrong, since coherence cannot be shorter than relaxation.
Both numbers are limited by the same mechanism, which is the fridge temperature.
Ninety microseconds of T1 is normal for this device; nothing there is faster than expected.
T2 shorter than T1 is entirely ordinary, and it is T2 above twice T1 that would be impossible.
The fridge limits thermal population, and a shared thermal limit would move both numbers together.
How good T2 could be
Work out the ceiling this T1 sets
Cryogenics & Vacuum
Okafor wants to know how much room there is before anybody spends a week chasing the noise. The relation is one over T2 equals one over twice T1 plus one over the pure dephasing time.
The dephasing rate is what is left when the relaxation contribution is subtracted, and it is the number worth chasing.
two independent loss processes add as rates rather than as times
Estimate the pure dephasing time behind these numbers.

Rates add; times do not. Energy loss contributes a dephasing rate of one over twice T1, because losing the energy also loses the phase, and whatever else is happening adds its own rate on top. Subtracting the first from the measured total leaves the pure dephasing rate, and its inverse is the time to quote when you go looking for the cause. If that number is far shorter than the T1 contribution, the fridge and the materials are not your problem this week — the wiring is.
About 39 µs.
T2 is 32 microseconds and T1 is 90. The relation is 1/T2 = 1/(2·T1) + 1/T_φ, so 1/T_φ = 1/32 − 1/180 per microsecond.
Choose the measured coherence time and the relaxation ceiling.

About thirty-nine microseconds, which is close enough to the measured T2 to say that dephasing is doing nearly all of the damage. T1 itself is an input to the ceiling rather than to this subtraction, and the pulse length and qubit count belong elsewhere.
1/T_φ = 1/T2 − 1/(2·T1), because the rates add and the relaxation contribution is the part you already know.
T2 is 32 µs
Twice T1 is 180 µs
What scrambles a phase without taking energy
Say where slow noise comes from
Fabrication & Materials
Lindqvist lists four candidates on the board and asks which of them changes a qubit's frequency slightly and slowly, rather than taking a quantum out of it.
Anything that shifts the qubit's frequency between one run and the next dephases it, even though it never takes energy.
a qubit's frequency can depend on its surroundings

Dephasing comes from the frequency wandering. If the qubit is a slightly different frequency on each repetition, the phase you accumulate differs each time, and averaging over repetitions washes the interference out — with no energy lost anywhere. Magnetic flux noise and current noise on a bias line both do exactly that. A two-level defect sitting at the qubit frequency is a different animal: it exchanges energy, so it hits T1. And thermal photons in the readout resonator shift the frequency at random, which is dephasing again and one of the commonest causes.
Dephasing — it moves the frequency without taking energy.
Dephasing, by the same route as flux noise.
Relaxation — it exchanges energy with the qubit.
Dephasing, and one of the commonest causes of it.
Flux noise moves the qubit frequency slightly between repetitions, which is dephasing.
Current noise on a bias line does the same thing by the same route.
A defect at the qubit frequency exchanges energy with it, so it shortens T1 rather than T2.
Stray photons in the readout resonator shift the frequency at random, which dephases without dissipating.
Magnetic flux noise through the loop.
Current noise on the bias line.
A two-level defect sitting at the qubit frequency.
Thermal photons left in the readout resonator.
One bit out
Understand what a readout actually decides, and how confident it is entitled to be.
The readout says 96 per cent fidelity. Nakamura says that number is doing a lot of work.

Tuesday, and the argument is about a single number. The single-shot readout fidelity is quoted at 96 per cent, and Ren Nakamura points out that it is the product of three separate things — how well the resonator separates the two states, how much noise the amplifier chain adds, and where somebody drew the line between them. Anders Holm wants each of the three measured. Priya Raghavan wants the headline figure for the review. Today you work out what the readout chain does to a signal, what a discriminator is actually deciding, and what part of that 96 per cent belongs to the qubit at all.
A readout number is a claim about a whole chain, and most of the chain has nothing to do with the qubit.
What happens between the chip and the answer
Follow the signal out
Control & Readout

Nakamura walks the chain: resonator, then a metre of cable, an isolator, a parametric amplifier at the mixing chamber, a semiconductor amplifier at 4 kelvin, more cable, a digitiser at room temperature.
The first amplifier sets the noise of the whole chain, which is why it is the coldest thing after the chip.
an amplifier increases a signal and adds noise of its own

Every stage after the first amplifier amplifies whatever the first one produced, noise included, so the first amplifier's own noise is what decides the signal-to-noise ratio of the whole chain. That is why it sits at the mixing chamber, cold and quiet, and why the warm electronics that follow it can be ordinary. Put the parametric amplifier at 4 kelvin instead and you can rebuild everything downstream to no effect at all.
The resonator, which shifts frequency depending on the qubit's state.
The parametric amplifier at the mixing chamber, which sets the noise of everything after it.
The semiconductor amplifier at 4 kelvin, which lifts the signal for the trip up.
The digitiser at room temperature, which records what arrives.
A line drawn between two clouds
Say what the discriminator decides
Control & Readout
The digitiser's shots plot as two clouds. Most are clearly in one or the other. A few thousand sit between them, and a line drawn somewhere in that gap assigns every one of those to a state.
A discriminator turns a continuous signal into a bit, and where the line sits decides which errors you make.
a measurement produces a distribution rather than a single value
What does moving the discriminator line do?

The line has to go somewhere, and wherever it goes, shots from one cloud that landed on the wrong side get called the other state. Move it toward the ground-state cloud and you misassign fewer excited shots and more ground ones; move it back and the trade reverses. The only thing that genuinely improves fidelity is separating the clouds — more signal, less noise, a longer integration — because the overlap is what sets the floor no line can beat.
It improves fidelity, because a better line assigns more shots correctly.
It trades one error for the other; the overlap sets the floor.
It has no effect, since the clouds are already separated.
It changes what the qubit does during readout.
A better-placed line reduces one error and increases the other; the sum is bounded by the overlap.
The clouds overlap by a few thousand shots, which is exactly the region the line has to cut.
The discriminator is applied after the measurement and cannot change what the qubit did.
Whose error is it
Take the readout out of the qubit number
Error & Verification
A circuit reports 8 per cent error. The readout on its own accounts for 4 per cent, and Holm wants to know what is left for the gates.
A quoted error is a sum until you separate the parts, and the interesting part is usually the smaller one.
errors from independent sources combine

Numbers that arrive as a single figure hide their parts, and this one has three. Readout error is measured on its own by preparing a known state and reading it back, and it is 4 per cent. State preparation is measured the same way and is small here. What is left is the gates, and it is the only part that a better circuit or a better calibration will move. Quoting the 8 per cent as gate error is the mistake that makes a machine look worse than it is; quoting 4 per cent as the whole error makes it look better.
Measured separately, and mostly about the amplifier chain.
Measured the same way, and small on this device.
The part a better pulse or calibration actually changes.
What a user sees, and the wrong number to work from.
Readout error is measurable on its own by preparing a known state and reading it straight back.
State preparation error is measured the same way and is small on this device.
Gate error is what is left after the other two, and it is the only part a recalibration moves.
The total is what a user experiences, and it is not the number that tells you what to fix.
Readout error, 4 per cent.
State preparation error, well under 1 per cent.
Gate error, whatever is left.
The 8 per cent total.
The offer with a date on it
Decide what to share, and when, while somebody else is deciding the same thing.
A group in Delft will run your circuit on their device this month, if they hear back by Friday.

Wednesday, and a note arrives from a group in Delft. They have a device of a different design and a window of machine time in ten days, and they will run Ridgeway's circuit on it if they get the pulse sequences by Friday. Anders Holm's instinct is to send nothing until the local numbers are settled, because a sequence sent out is a result you no longer control. Priya Raghavan points out that this is the second device he has been asking for since March, offered free, with a deadline. This morning she is right, and the caution would cost the group the one thing it has been missing. Today you decide what to send, what to hold, and what you would need back to call it a replication.
Some evidence has a window on it, and refusing to move inside that window is a decision with its own cost.
What you would need back
Decide what makes a replication worth the name
Error & Verification
Holm writes down what Delft would have to return for the run to count as a check rather than a courtesy. Raghavan writes down what she is willing to send by Friday.
A replication has to be able to fail, which means the other group needs the method and not the expected answer.
a second measurement is only a check if it could disagree

The value of an independent run is that it shares as little as possible with the original. The circuit and the pulse sequences have to go, or they are running a different experiment.
